summary: This standards-track RFC describes how to signal MAC address withdrawal over a static pseudowire, using the pseudowire associated channel. This is needed in VPLS and H-VPLS deployments where pseudowires are statically provisioned, so that stale MAC entries can be cleared when the topology changes.

eli5.summary: If a person moves house, the post office needs to forget their old address. This is a message that tells everyone to erase the old entry.

questions: how does mac withdraw work over static pseudowire
what is the r-bit in mac withdraw
what is the retransmit time for mac withdraw
subtitle: How a pseudowire endpoint tells its peers to forget MAC addresses when signaling over LDP is not available.

tldr.problem: When a pseudowire (PW) fails over, other nodes keep stale MAC address entries and traffic is blackholed. The usual LDP-based MAC withdrawal cannot be used on statically provisioned PWs.
tldr.mechanism: A new PW OAM message, sent in-band on the PW Associated Channel, carries a sequence-numbered MAC withdrawal. The receiver must acknowledge every message, and the sender retransmits until it gets an ACK.
tldr.outcome: Static PWs in VPLS and H-VPLS can clear stale MACs quickly. It is best effort: if the signal is lost, MAC relearning or aging out eventually restores traffic.

today: RFC 7769 is a Proposed Standard, published in February 2016. No obsoleting or updating RFCs are recorded for it.

sections.title: Why Static PWs Need Their Own Withdrawal
sections.content:
RFC 4762 defines an LDP-based MAC address withdrawal. A node sends an LDP Address Withdraw Message with a MAC List TLV, and other Provider Edge nodes remove those dynamically learned MAC addresses. RFC 7361 adds an optimized form that removes only the addresses that need to be relearned in H-VPLS networks.

A PW can be signaled with LDP or statically provisioned. On a static PW the LDP mechanism cannot be used. This RFC follows the approach of RFC 6478, which carries PW status over the in-band PW Associated Channel, and uses a PW OAM message to withdraw MAC addresses learned over a static PW.
sections.eli5: Some pathways have a built-in loudspeaker for announcements, and some do not. This RFC gives the ones without a loudspeaker a way to pass notes instead.

sections.title: Best Effort, With Fallbacks
sections.content:
MAC withdraw signaling is a best effort scheme. It tries to speed up network convergence by reducing blackholes caused by PW failover for protected PWs. The protocol handles possible loss of the signal due to congestion, but does not guarantee delivery, just as with LDP-based signaling.

If the signal never arrives, traffic resumes by other means: MAC relearning from bi-directional traffic, or, as a last resort, aging out of MAC addresses when no frames arrive from those sources. These fallbacks cause temporary blackouts but do not leave the network permanently unusable.
sections.eli5: If your note gets lost, people will eventually notice the kid moved anyway. It just takes longer, and some mail goes to the wrong desk in the meantime.

sections.title: The MAC Withdraw OAM Message
sections.content:
Unlike LDP, static PWs have no reliable transport, so this design relies on retransmissions and acknowledgements. Here the ACK is mandatory. The message follows the RFC 6478 guidelines: the first 4 bytes of the OAM header, then a message-specific field and a set of TLVs.

The message MUST contain a Sequence Number TLV, and it MUST be the first TLV; otherwise the whole message is dropped. It MAY also carry the MAC Flush Parameter TLV from RFC 7361 for H-VPLS and PBB-VPLS. The MAC List TLV follows the rules of RFC 4762. The channel type is 0x28 and the Sequence Number TLV type is 0x1.

Two flag bits matter. The A-bit is set by a receiver to acknowledge a message, and an acknowledgement leaves out the MAC TLVs. The R-bit asks the peer to reset sequence numbers; a sender sets it when the PW has restarted and has no record of earlier sequence numbers.
sections.eli5: Each note has a number on it, a box to tick that says "this is my reply", and a box that says "let's start counting from the beginning again".

sections.title: Sequence Numbers
sections.content: Because the OAM channel has no reliable transport, sequence numbers let the receiver tell a new message from a retransmitted old one. The scheme comes from RFC 4385 with two differences: the Sequence Number field is 32 bits, and overflow detection is simpler. A sequence number above 2,147,483,647 (0x7FFFFFFF) counts as an overflow and is reset to 1.
sections.eli5: Numbering the notes lets you spot a copy of an old note you already read. If the counter gets too big, it starts again at 1.

sections.title: Sender and Receiver Behavior
sections.content:
The sender keeps a transmit counter per PW. Each new set of MAC TLVs increments it and the new number goes in the message. The counter starts at 1, so the first withdraw message sent after initialization carries 2. The sender waits for an ACK for the Retransmit Time, 1 second by default or a configured value, then resends with the same sequence number. Retransmission MUST stop when an ACK arrives, and a way to suppress endless retransmission MUST be implemented. One second with two retries is RECOMMENDED, but intervals, retry counts and an increasing backoff are local matters. If a newer withdraw message is needed, the sender MUST drop retransmission of the older one and only retries the latest.

The receiver keeps an expected-sequence register per PW, initialized to 1. If an arriving sequence number is greater than the register, it removes the MAC addresses and updates the register. It then sends an ACK carrying the same sequence number. If the number is smaller than or equal to the register, the MAC TLVs are not processed, but an ACK with that number MUST still be sent. An ACK counts for all messages up to that sequence number.

If a PW is deleted and re-added or the router restarts, the node may forget its sequence number and the peer would ignore its messages. The first MAC withdraw then sets the R-bit. A receiver MUST reset its send and receive sequence numbers first, then process the message, and send the ACK with the R-bit cleared.
sections.eli5: The sender keeps knocking until someone says "got it", but only for its latest message. The listener answers every knock, even repeats, but only acts on a note it has not seen before.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The security section is a single sentence: the measures described in RFC 4447, RFC 5085 and RFC 6073 are adequate for this mechanism.

IANA assigned channel type 0x0028 ("MAC Withdraw OAM Message") from the MPLS Generalized Associated Channel (G-ACh) Types registry, and TLV type 0x0001 ("Sequence Number TLV") from the LDP TLV Type Name Space registry.
sections.eli5: The authors say the safety rules already used for these pathways are good enough. Two new labels were registered so nobody else reuses them.
